Exploring Chicago Public School Data with SQL and Python¶

By Mohammad Sayem Chowdhury

Welcome! In this notebook, I'll share my personal journey analyzing the Chicago Public Schools dataset using SQL and Python. My goal is to uncover insights, practice SQL skills, and reflect on the process as I go. Let's dive in!

My Objectives¶

  • Get familiar with the Chicago Public Schools performance dataset
  • Load the data into a database for SQL analysis
  • Explore table and column metadata
  • Tackle real-world questions using SQL
  • Share my thoughts and findings throughout the process

Chicago Public Schools - Progress Report Cards (2011-2012)¶

The city of Chicago released a dataset showing all school level performance data used to create School Report Cards for the 2011-2012 school year.

About the Dataset¶

The dataset covers school-level performance data for Chicago Public Schools in the 2011-2012 year. It includes a wide range of metrics, from attendance to college enrollment. I downloaded a database-friendly CSV version for this analysis.

Before jumping in, I took some time to review the columns and get a sense of what information is available. This step always helps me plan my analysis and think about interesting questions to ask.

Loading the Data¶

I prefer to load CSV data into a database for more flexible querying. While pandas makes it easy, I like to use the database's own tools for better control over data types. For this project, I used the database console's LOAD tool to create a table called SCHOOLS and import the data. This gives me a solid foundation for SQL analysis.

Connecting to My Database¶

With the data loaded, it's time to connect to the database using the ipython-sql extension. This lets me run SQL queries directly from my notebook, which I find super convenient.

In [ ]:
# Loading the SQL extension so I can run SQL queries in this notebook
%load_ext sql
In [ ]:
# Enter the connection string for your Db2 on Cloud database instance below
# %sql ibm_db_sa://my-username:my-password@my-hostname:my-port/my-db-name
# Replace with your actual connection string for the database
%sql ibm_db_sa://
Out[ ]:
'Connected: bsx51096@BLUDB'

Checking My Table¶

I always like to confirm that my table was created successfully. I'll query the system catalog to list all tables in my schema and make sure SCHOOLS is there.

In [ ]:
# Checking which tables exist in my schema
%sql select TABSCHEMA,TABNAME,CREATE_TIME from SYSCAT.TABLES WHERE TABSCHEMA = 'BSX51096'

 * ibm_db_sa://bsx51096:***@dashdb-txn-sbox-yp-dal09-14.services.dal.bluemix.net:50000/BLUDB
Done.

Exploring Table Columns¶

Next, I want to see how many columns the SCHOOLS table has. This helps me understand the dataset's complexity and plan my queries.

In [ ]:
# Counting the number of columns in the SCHOOLS table
%sql select count(*) from SYSCAT.COLUMNS where tabname='SCHOOLS';

 * ibm_db_sa://bsx51096:***@dashdb-txn-sbox-yp-dal09-14.services.dal.bluemix.net:50000/BLUDB
Done.
Out[ ]:
1
78

Double-click here for the solution.

Now, I'll list all columns in the SCHOOLS table, along with their data types and lengths. This gives me a detailed view of the table structure.

In [ ]:
# Listing all columns, their types, and lengths in the SCHOOLS table
%sql select COLNAME, TYPENAME, LENGTH from SYSCAT.COLUMNS where TABNAME = 'SCHOOLS'

Done.

Some Quick Questions¶

  • Is the column name for "SCHOOL ID" in upper or mixed case?
  • What is the exact name of the "Community Area Name" column? Any spaces?
  • Are there columns where spaces or parentheses have been replaced by underscores?

I like to answer these by inspecting the column list above. It's always interesting to see how data is structured!

My Problem-Solving Section¶

Now for the fun part—solving real questions with SQL! I'll share my thought process and any interesting findings along the way.

Problem 1¶

How many Elementary Schools are in the dataset?¶
In [ ]:
### Problem 1: Counting Elementary Schools

How many elementary schools are in the dataset? I want to see how many schools are classified as 'ES' (Elementary School).

%sql SELECT COUNT(*) FROM SCHOOLS WHERE "Elementary, Middle, or High School" = 'ES'

 * ibm_db_sa://bsx51096:***@dashdb-txn-sbox-yp-dal09-14.services.dal.bluemix.net:50000/BLUDB
Done.
Out[ ]:
1
462

Double-click here for the solution.

Problem 2: Highest Safety Score¶

I'm curious—what's the highest safety score among all schools? Let's find out!

In [42]:
%sql SELECT MAX(safety_score) FROM SCHOOLS;

 * ibm_db_sa://bsx51096:***@dashdb-txn-sbox-yp-dal09-14.services.dal.bluemix.net:50000/BLUDB
Done.
Out[42]:
1
99

Problem 4: Top 10 Schools by Student Attendance¶

Which schools have the highest average student attendance? I'll list the top 10 to see who leads in this area.

In [47]:
%sql select Name_of_School, Average_Student_Attendance from SCHOOLS \
    order by Average_Student_Attendance desc nulls last limit 10

Problem 5: Lowest Student Attendance¶

On the flip side, which 5 schools have the lowest average student attendance? I'll sort them in ascending order to find out.

In [51]:
%sql SELECT Name_of_School, Average_Student_Attendance  \
     from SCHOOLS \
     order by Average_Student_Attendance \

Problem 6: Cleaning Up Attendance Data¶

I noticed the attendance column includes a '%' sign. Let's remove it for cleaner analysis.

In [53]:
%sql SELECT Name_of_School, REPLACE(Average_Student_Attendance,'%','')\
     from SCHOOLS \
     order by Average_Student_Attendance \
     fetch first 5 rows only

 * ibm_db_sa://bsx51096:***@dashdb-txn-sbox-yp-dal09-14.services.dal.bluemix.net:50000/BLUDB
Done.
Out[53]:
name_of_school 2

Barbara Vick Early Childhood & Family Center 60.90
Dyett High School 62.50
Wendell Phillips Academy High School 63.00
Orr Academy High School 66.30

Problem 7: Schools with Low Attendance¶

Which schools have an average student attendance below 70%? This could highlight schools that need extra support.

In [58]:
%sql SELECT Name_of_School, Average_Student_Attendance  \
     from SCHOOLS \
     where DECIMAL ( REPLACE(Average_Student_Attendance, '%', '') ) < 70 \
     order by Average_Student_Attendance

Problem 8: College Enrollment by Community Area¶

I'm interested in the total college enrollment for each community area. This can reveal which areas send the most students to college.

In [59]:
%sql select Community_Area_Name, sum(College_Enrollment) AS TOTAL_ENROLLMENT \
   from SCHOOLS \
   group by Community_Area_Name

Problem 9: Least College Enrollment¶

Which 5 community areas have the lowest total college enrollment? I'll sort them in ascending order to find out.

In [69]:
%sql select Community_Area_Name, sum(College_Enrollment) AS TOTAL_ENROLLMENT \
   from SCHOOLS \
   group by Community_Area_Name \
order by total_enrollment asc\

Problem 10: Hardship Index for a Specific Community Area¶

I want to find the hardship index for the community area with a college enrollment of 4638. This could reveal interesting correlations.

In [72]:
%%sql 
select hardship_index 
   from chicago_socioeconomic_data CD, schools CPS 
   where CD.ca = CPS.community_area_number 
      and college_enrollment = 4368

Problem 11: Hardship Index for the Top College Enrollment Area¶

Finally, I'll get the hardship index for the community area with the highest college enrollment. This might show if high enrollment correlates with lower hardship.

In [73]:
%sql select ca, community_area_name, hardship_index from chicago_socioeconomic_data \
   where ca in \
   ( select community_area_number from schools order by college_enrollment desc limit 1 )

My Reflections¶

Working through this dataset has been a rewarding experience. I learned how to handle real-world data quirks, query columns with tricky names, and use SQL functions to answer meaningful questions. Each problem gave me new insights into Chicago's schools, and I enjoyed sharing my thought process along the way.
